title: Shared Metadata Proxy — Multi-Tenant Isolation Failure via Tenant Header
description: In multi-tenant cloud environments, a shared metadata proxy provides instance metadata (credentials, configuration) to tenants. Tenant isolation relies on request headers (e.g., X-Tenant-ID, X-Project-ID). If the header is attacker-controlled and not independently validated, cross-tenant credential theft is possible. Attack: (1) Discover the metadata proxy endpoint — common at dedicated metadata IPs (169.254.169.254) or internal service URLs in multi-tenant setups. (2) Probe with your own tenant ID to confirm functionality: curl -H 'X-Tenant-ID: my-tenant' http://PROXY/latest/meta-data/. (3) Enumerate other tenants: brute force or enumerate tenant IDs from other sources (error messages, shared dashboards, naming conventions). (4) Access another tenant's metadata: curl -H 'X-Tenant-ID: other-tenant' http://PROXY/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/. (5) Extract other tenant's cloud credentials (AWS AccessKeyId/SecretAccessKey, Azure MSI token, GCP SA token). (6) Use stolen credentials to access the victim tenant's cloud resources: S3, RDS, DynamoDB, etc. (7) This attack is effective against multi-tenant platforms that share a metadata proxy between tenants and rely on HTTP headers for tenant routing.
techniques: Discover metadata proxy: probe 169.254.169.254, metadata.internal, or discover from service documentation
Probe with tenant header: curl -H 'X-Tenant-ID: my-tenant' http://PROXY/latest/meta-data/
Enumerate tenants: brute-force tenant IDs from predictable patterns (tenant-001, tenant-002, ...)
Use stolen credentials: export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=... AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=... AWS_SESSION_TOKEN=...
Verify cross-tenant access: aws sts get-caller-identity, aws s3 ls
Try different header names: X-Project-ID, X-Tenant-Name, X-Account-ID, X-Subscription-ID
indicators: Multi-tenant environment (shared IP space, tenant portals)
Metadata proxy endpoint accessible from multiple tenants
X-Tenant-ID or similar tenant routing header in requests
IMDS or WireServer accessible with different tenant IDs
prerequisites: Access to a tenant in the multi-tenant environment
Ability to set custom HTTP headers in requests
Target tenant ID or predictable tenant naming scheme
